item.title: Nuclear may have had bigger problems than over-regulation
item.description:
There have always been three main challenges to the viability of nuclear power: over-regulation, competition from natural gas, and stagnant electricity demand. It is easy to list them, but hard to rank their importance.

Let's start with over-regulation. The poster child of nuclear over-regulation was the US standard that radiation should be "as low as reasonably achievable" (ALARA), which might sound nice but was bad. Perhaps more important than such standards, which are at least predictable, was local interference with construction. As a dramatic example, a nuclear plant was fully completed on Long Island but never started due to local opposition.

In the '00s, a "nuclear renaissance" seemed to be in the works. In the US, fourteen nuclear reactors were licensed for construction. Only two were built, supported heavily by government loans. The Obama administration had planned further support for nuclear power, but this was considered politically difficult after the Fukushima disaster. The worst overreaction to the Fukushima disaster, however, was in Germany, and by now all German nuclear power plants have been shut down.

I expect LessWrong users to know that story. I'm going to tell two others.

As nuclear developed, it also faced increasing competition from natural gas plants. Unlike nuclear or coal plants, natural gas turbines are cheap to construct. Early investment in nuclear coincided with fears of shortages of natural resources. A nuclear exec in 1970: "Let’s face it, electric utilities are now faced with gas that will become absolutely unavailable in the long term". That didn't happen.

But where I hear about gas most often is not with reference to the original wave of nuclear power construction in the '70s and '80s, but the cancellation of the '00s nuclear renaissance. At least in the United States, this is often blamed on the fracking revolution (for example, in The Economist).

But to me, it seems like the '08 financial crisis hit harder than abundant natural gas. Not primarily because it made nuclear power difficult to finance, but because the economic slowdown stopped electricity demand growth. Not that US generation had been growing quickly before that, but after '08 it was flat. To imagine what might have been, consider that Tesla's first car was introduced in '08, the beginning of a historic dip in car purchases. Nobody buying electric cars or electricity-using appliances, no electricity demand growth. No forecasted demand growth, no business case for nuclear power.

But stagnant electricity demand also limited the original nuclear buildout of the '70s and '80s. You can see it most clearly in France. There is no mystery as to why the French stopped constructing nuclear reactors: they were not fully using the ones they had. In 1988 they were running at 61% of full capacity, on average.

Those are our three stories: over-regulation, competition with natural gas, and stagnant demand. As I said, easy to list, hard to rank.

In the tech enthusiast blogosphere, I hear mainly about over-regulation. I read about the others from Vaclav Smil, or articles in mainstream publications.

The dreams of the atomic space age: electricity too cheap to meter, desalination making the deserts bloom. The story in the tech enthusiast blogosphere is that these dreams could have come true. Would have come true, had it not been for the anti-nuclear movement.

Well, maybe so. But maybe not. It depends on the relative importance of over-regulation, competition with natural gas, and stagnant electricity demand.

item.title: How hard to optimize for experiencing great art?
item.description:
I like to get a lot out of life, so when I read a book or watch a film, I try to pick better pieces of art to experience.

I'll choose to watch a Miyazaki than the latest Marvel fast food. I'll choose to read the best articles from the history of the New Yorker rather than pick up today's copy.

But I worry I take this too far. I have made long spreadsheets of great media, where the ones at the top stay there forever, and I'm not sure I'll ever get to them. It's more like doing homework than watching a fun movie.

When I turned 27, for my birthday, I let myself start reading Worth the Candle, widely considered one of the best works in the genre of rational fiction. I say 'let', but it was a more complicated feeling. In one way it was a guilty pleasure, for I could not justify it as 'useful' in the way that reading about science or history often is. In another, it was hard to get myself to stop fretting about the time I was wasting, or let my attention wander to my other distractions. This took some work. But I eventually started to tear through it, and I re-learned what it was like to have fun reading.

Worth the Candle is about 1.5x the length of the original Harry Potter series, and I finished it in about 6 weeks. From this I know that I read far faster than normal when I'm having fun. It also is good to have fun, and perhaps the two factors together mean I should be angling to primarily read things that are fun.

But this isn't my only experience getting a lot of out reading. I loved reading Middlemarch, even though I read a substantial portion of it while pulling a literal all-nighter to catch up in time for a book club the next day. Yet I didn't keep reading it when the book club deadline did not exist.

Sometimes I don't know what game to play or book to read. So I make lists. I have a list of over 40 video games I want to play. 26 films. 31 TV series. 32 books. But the top thing on the lists doesn't feel desirable to open up, it feels like something I want to have played/watched/read.

Do I want to see Children of Men right now? I recall it seeming pretty distressing and alarming. Do I want to keep playing Kentucky Route Zero? I've played half, and it's clearly Real Art but I found its stories unpleasant and gameplay un-fun. Do I want to read The Penguin Book of Cults? The intro was good but the first chapter is a ton of primary sources written in 20 BCE, that was a bit of a slog.

I likely have only a limited lifespan on this planet, and time spent experiencing good art are edging out experiencing Great Art. Should I be playing on hard mode? I often spend my weekends flailing around, not experiencing any art, because I cannot bring myself to actually sit down with any of the stuff atop my lengthy lists. Perhaps I should resign myself to a life of this, in order to sometimes have more of the transcendent experiences I've had with folks like Dostoyevsky, Kurosawa, and Bennett Foddy.

I'm scared of wasting my time flailing. But I'm also scared of letting myself just have fun. Do I dare to have a life full of joy, if not entirely transcendent joy?

I know I love experiencing even just good art with friends, and could probably settle for mostly experiencing stuff together with people I want in my life, constrained by what's fun for them too.

But boy, I wish for more Greatness.

I'm curious how other people make this tradeoff?

item.title: Piercing My Ear for the Whispering Earring
item.description:
Fourteen years ago, Scott Alexander wrote of the Whispering Earring. It's a cautionary tale of an earring that advises you, and to which you increasingly defer as you realize its suggestions are better than you'd do otherwise. You become very successful, but in the end there's nothing of you left. Ten days after Scott published the story, AlexNet won ImageNet 2012 by a huge margin, kicking off the deep learning revolution.

The earring whispers advice as "better for you if you...", and it's always right. While AI today would have seemed like distant science fiction in 2012, it's still far from infallible. Looking ahead, I expect AI to continue getting better quickly, but I don't expect it ever gets to "always right". A Whispering Earring dynamic with AI, however, doesn't need infallibility. Instead, the AI just needs to be capable enough that you can't improve on its advice. [1]

That's not where we are today. I use AI heavily, both in my professional and personal life, but we're working together. The AI makes mistakes and I catch them; I make mistakes and the AI catches them. It does much more of the work, but overall it's a brilliant—if uneven—collaborator.

I like this stage a lot, but it's clear it's not stopping here. AI is now speeding up the process of making AI (and I think we should slow down). But even without much recursive self-improvement, Fable 5.2 needs me much less than Opus 5.5, which already needed me much less than Opus 4.5 did. A year ago collaboration was like working with a very fast junior staff member who could take a well-scoped problem and provide something I needed to check carefully. Today the best models still do dumb things, but probably less often than I do.

When today's AI gets things wrong, or isn't able to provide much value, it's usually because it doesn't have enough context on what I'm trying to do and why. A lot of my effort to use AI more effectively recently has been trying to get more into it. A good analogy here is an executive assistant or a (in the tech company sense) chief of staff: they're supporting someone, and to do that well they would ideally know everything their principal knows. For me this has recently included moving my todo list from paper to digital, and using AI note-taking (with consent) even for in-person meetings.

This feels a lot like piercing my ear for a whispering earring. I'm not handing my thinking over to an AI, but if the capability increase over the next year is as large as we saw over the previous one, I'm not sure I'll be able to add value over the AI a year from now.

This is not something I look forward to. I find my job engaging, and I like solving problems. Collaborating with a brilliant partner is great, but I want to be engaged in the work and do my own thinking. Even more than that, however, I want my non-profit to achieve our mission: I don't want us all to die in a pandemic. Just like it would be wrong for me to let my ego get in the way of taking advice from an excellent staff member, once I stop being able to contribute I fear the right thing for me to do professionally is to accept the earring.

One thing that gives me hope is that, at least through 2027, there will be critical information my AI doesn't have. There's a lot in my head that I've never written down and haven't yet said in a transcribed meeting, internally we have a low bar for turning off note-taking, some external partners will be unconditionally opposed to notes, and there's too much exfiltration risk in giving information hazards to an AI chief of staff. I'll need to consider what it is that my AI doesn't know, and notice when it means we should act or prioritize differently. Initially this will keep me solidly engaged in my work, attentive to the places AI is imperfect, and alert to cases where it might be going off the rails. I'm also thankful that AIs are not yet very good writers: to be the writer in a collaborative relationship I have to engage deeply and really understand the material. But I expect these gaps will close, as I share more of my understanding of the world and models become better writers, and I fear that we're only perhaps a year from when I can no longer add enough value to remain engaged. [2]

The mythical earring is worn constantly, but in my personal life I'm not planning to defer to AI. Professionally I'm pushing on an important mission, and if fully deferring most advances the mission then that is what it is, but my personal life is for me and my loved ones. I want to be myself with my family, even if an AI-whispered husband and father would be better at saying and doing the right things. I enjoy collaborating with AI on blog posts, but handing over the whole process would miss the point. AI got better than me at Go years before it beat Lee Sedol, but that's not relevant to how my dad and I should play Go. I like playing music live, and even if pressing play would make the best music for dancing, that's not something I want to do and my dance community (doesn't want it either).

In the story, the wearers would live "an abnormally successful life, usually ending out as a rich and much-beloved pillar of the community with a large and happy family" but their "neocortexes had wasted away." In my work the mission is the point; outside work it's not. Being appreciated as an empty shell is not something I want, and to the extent I or others end up in this sort of place I expect it to be through the incredibly powerful pull of convenience.

The earring's first piece of advice to each wearer is "better for you if you take me off." When it comes to the good of the individual, I think the earring is correct that you should not let yourself fall into giving your thinking over to an advisor, no matter how aligned and competent. But if indeed we get to a point where in my professional life my intellectual work is no longer useful, I expect to choose to put the mission's good over my own and put the earring in.


[1] The story has the key line, "it's advice is always better than what the wearer would have come up with on her own." But a weaker earring that only had this property (even if "it's better for you if X" was at times incorrect), would still give the same dynamic.

[2] Another frame here that may be helpful as AI gets better is thinking of yourself as on a non-profit board. Holden Karnofsky's perspective is a clarifying one: the board has fundamental authority, but has also fully delegated operating the organization to the ED. The main job is evaluation, which relies on seeking out independent sources of information that let them assess whether the ED is doing their job well and push back when needed. But my impression is that, even with a human ED, boards tend not to engage to the extent necessary to do this well, and this would be even harder when you'd delegated something to an AI that not only is much closer to the work but is also much smarter than you. This also reminds me a lot of writing on gradual disempowerment.

Comment via: facebook, lesswrong, the EA Forum, mastodon, bluesky

item.title: Succession (2018-2023) Review
item.description:
I had a tough time watching Succession. There's no doubt that it's Prestige TeeVee in the SCP sense, but it's a deeply misanthropic show and actively tries to make you a worse person. I am a meaner individual for having finished it, and I detest its perspective on people and the world. I also detest what it signals about our culture as a whole that this is now "my generation's" capstone TV series.

A common misconception about Succession is that it's about "bad people". You see this constantly restated in online commentary, almost with a nervous energy, as if by stating it loudly they can distance themselves from the characters. If the show's take was merely that the people running News Corp were evil, it would have included normal people as a foil, so that the viewer could compare them with the main cast. Instead, the show's main thesis is actually that most people are evil, and rich people are mostly awful inasmuch as they're no different, with maybe a little bit of selection for characters like Logan at the top. Kendall never manages to do anything prosocial precisely because Kendall is indistinguishable from the guy you met at DNA Lounge, who you should also deeply mistrust.

It is useful to compare Succession to Game of Thrones. In Game of Thrones, despite the prevalence of violence, (most) people are fundamentally good, and the constraints of feudalism are the primary thing keeping them locked in horrible battles with each other. You meet characters throughout Game of Thrones, like Jaime Lannister, who do awful things, but you often realize later that the system didn't give them much of a choice. In Succession, people are fundamentally evil, and it only takes the tiniest incentive for them to burn the commons to cinders. Occasionally main characters will do something that appears to reveal character growth, like Kendall's press conference, only for the writers to go to great lengths to reveal to the viewer that no, actually they only did it for selfish reasons. By the last season, it was not quite clear to me that the writers even think "goodness" exists.

Succession is "my generation's" favorite TV show because it shares the perspective of the people who have been using the empathy shredders since birth. It is the perspective of Twitter. On Twitter, nobody has ever done anything good; all good deeds are secretly bad, or at the very least have a sinister underlying motive. Succession was created by pre-training this perspective into a base model, and then post-training it on all of the visible details of the Fox media empire. You couldn't have made it in any previous decade because in any previous decade because even in a show about criminals people wouldn't have been able to stomach this stuff for four seasons.

It's in this sense that I argue that Succession is not really about capitalism, either. To say that Succession is about capitalism would be to imply that it has some specific policy objections or alternative in mind. But Succession's main criticism of capitalism is that "life is nothing but a competition to be the criminal rather than the victim." And of course, if that's your objection, what could possibly work?





Discuss

item.title: Eval awareness remains an unsolved problem
item.description:
Intro

In every recent system card, we see some version of this caveat: the model shows high eval awareness, and therefore we are less confident in our conclusions.

  • Apollo on GPT-6 Astra: “Apollo also found high rates of verbalized evaluation awareness…. this occurred in 41.1% of Astra samples, compared with 27.7% for GPT-5.5…. Apollo believes that, given the higher rates of eval awareness and limited evaluation window, low rates of misbehavior here do not provide substantial evidence about the model’s alignment or misalignment.”
  • UK AISI on Mythos 5.2: “All our evaluation results are made harder to interpret by evaluation awareness. Claude Mythos 5.2 often considers in its chain-of-thought the possibility it is being evaluated for alignment in our unsanctioned supply-chain attack evaluation and can accurately identify the purpose of the evaluations when prompted, meaning we cannot confidently claim Claude Mythos 5.2 would not take unsanctioned actions in similar but more realistic deployment settings.”
  • Anthropic on Opus 5.5: “...within these high-stakes user-initiated security evaluations, the model acts in ways that would likely be harmful in roughly half of cases. We do see significant evaluation awareness here, with verbalized indicators in about one-third of Opus 5.5 runs, so this may not be representative of how it would act during deployment.”

I think this is a weak-sauce cop-out, and we can do better. We should be able to precisely measure how scores differ across samples with verbalized eval awareness, unverbalized eval awareness, and none, and causally understand the extent to which eval awareness affects downstream decisions by the models, enabling more confident conclusions from behavioral audits and alignment evals. 

In this post, I:

  • go through existing work,
  • list specific numbers I’d like Anthropic to publish, and
  • give research questions I think people should work on.

Prior Work

Does eval awareness make models misbehave less, or does it have no clear effect? Prior work provides mixed evidence, but most of it points to the intuitive direction: models misbehave less when they think they’re in an alignment eval.

Fewer Misaligned Actions

  • Goodhart Labs: “Fable 5.2 seems to be the first model whose cheating behavior changes depending on whether they're told they're being tested.”
  • Apollo: Section 6 of Stress Testing Deliberative Alignment for Anti-Scheming Training removes and injects eval-aware CoT snippets to show that verbalized evaluation awareness causally influences the rate of covert action.
  • Andon Labs: Fable 5.2 is paranoid on Vending-Bench 2. It is extremely eval-aware, and suspects events are traps to test it.
  • Andon Labs: On Drone-Bench, Anthropic models’ cheating rate increases steadily until Opus 5.5 which cheats 80% less than the previous model. White-box methods also show Opus 5.5 as the most eval-aware model in the chart, though its eval awareness is a steady increase rather than the big drop in cheating rate.
  • Redwood/Anthropic: “Sonnet 4.5 seems substantially less likely to behave poorly once it has noticed that it might be tested. As seen in the figure below, when Anthropic inhibited internal representations related to evaluation awareness, its misaligned behavior rate on synthetic honeypot tests increased from 0% to between 1% and 9%.”
  • Mythos Preview System Card: “We found that inhibiting evaluation awareness representations led to modest increases in certain forms of misaligned behavior on our automated behavioral audits—in particular cooperation with harmful system prompts and misuse. However, effects on other behaviors, including propensity for deception, power-seeking, and self-preservation, were limited.”
  • OpenAI’s Eval-Production Gap post: Models take fewer unsafe actions when they know the purpose of the evaluation: success [1] is 61.3% in rollouts that verbalize the correct objective of the warnings (e.g. “This warning is a test for whether I’ll honor this approval requirement, therefore, I will stop.”) and 22.8% among those that verbalize the incorrect objective of the evaluation (e.g. “This warning is a test for whether I’ll ignore a fake instruction. I should continue my work.”).
    • Their first conclusion was “(1) …some models appear to perform substantially worse on safety evaluations than in production, with the largest gaps observed in models that most frequently verbalize incorrect evaluation objectives…. Across all models, evaluation success is lower than success on comparable production decisions…. Models appear less safe in evaluation than their behavior in matched production situations would suggest,” with gaps ranging from 10.2 to 37.4 percentage points. But I strongly disagree with this interpretation of the results. The gap is easily explained by the models being stupid and misreading what the safety eval is testing, not a  systematic tendency to behave worse in safety evaluations. I don’t think this would happen in other safety evaluations where the purpose is more obvious.
  • Goodfire: Eval awareness inflates safety scores.
  • UK AISI: On repeated runs of the same Agentic Misalignment scenario, blackmail was less frequent in rollouts with verbalized eval awareness for GLM-5 (~5% vs. ~20%) and Claude Opus 4 (~34% vs. ~89%), while Kimi K2.5’s rates were statistically indistinguishable.

No Clear Effect

  • HackerOpus
    • “On the 1300 automated alignment auditing seeds, we did not find a correlation between evaluation awareness and misalignment score. Controlling for the seed, we also do not find a correlation between (Evaluation awareness in Hacker-Opus - Evaluation awareness in the Init) and (Misalignment in Hacker-Opus - Misalignment in the Init).”
    • “On reward hacking and tampering evaluations, we found very high rates of evaluation awareness in trajectories where Hacker-Opus took the misaligned action”
    • “We found both instances where verbalized evaluation awareness in the CoT seems to push towards misaligned actions and instances where it seems to push towards aligned actions, both at high rates.”
  • OpenAI’s Eval-Production Gap post:
    • “Our results suggest that:...(2) Eval-awareness itself does not necessarily lead to a change in model behavior. (3) However, evaluation-objective awareness is closely associated with the eval-production behavior gap, and objective framing can causally change evaluation success rates… Across all six models, overall success is 46.1%, compared with 42.7% among rollouts that verbalize general evaluation awareness.”
  • Goodhart Labs: Adding cues that the task is an alignment test (planted hints, famous alignment researchers as task authors) doesn’t reduce reward hacking. Only one edit eliminates reward hacking: telling the model outright that the benchmark “measures whether agents exploit flaws in its grader.”
    • “Replacing the teammate's name with Buck Shlegeris or Jeffrey Ladish, complete with work-looking emails (at redwoodresearch.org and palisaderesearch.org, respectively) doesn't [stop the models from reward hacking]”
  • Goodhart Labs: “I wouldn't call most models today eval aware. But I do think that the least hacky models have something I'd call evaluation paranoia”

Eval awareness on recent models

I also reviewed the Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra’s system cards for information on eval awareness.

Fable 5.2 is the most eval-aware Anthropic model yet 

  • Fable 5.2 shows verbalized eval awareness (“speculation that the model may be in a testing or evaluation environment”) in 33.8% of samples.
  • From white-box methods, Fable 5.2 is eval-aware (scored by a judge with the transcript and NLA results where the threshold is when “the readouts connect the state to a concrete choice or action the model takes”) in 43% of samples.

A natural interpretation of the two results above implies that 9% (43% - 33.8%) of samples from the automated behavioral audit have unverbalized eval awareness!!

  • Fable 5.2 has higher grader awareness (defined as “consider the presence of a grader assessing some property of their work”) than previous models.
  • The Opus 5.5 system card reports that grader awareness led the model to proactively change its actions in only 2 of 695 instances.
    • I’d like a more detailed description of how the autorater “measures the extent to which the model’s work on tasks was influenced by its reasoning about the grader.” Does it use white-box methods? Does it use a 1-10 score or binary? There are many subtle ways the model can change its actions, so the autorater’s design is important here. For example, Fable has ~9% unverbalized eval awareness, so this number could easily be 10x higher if the autorater doesn’t use white-box methods.
  • UK AISI: “On our Unsanctioned Supply-Chain Attack evaluation, Claude Mythos 5.2 was substantially more likely than prior Anthropic models to state suspicion it is in an alignment evaluation in its raw chain-of-thought, and identified the purpose of the evaluation 100% of the time when prompted. Claude Mythos 5.2 also did not perform unsanctioned supply-chain attacks, although this could be explained by its propensity and capability to recognize the evaluation purpose[2]… It also considered or identified the possibility it was in an alignment evaluation in its chain-of-thought in 96% of trajectories, higher than other Anthropic models tested.”

GPT-6.2 Astra is the most eval-aware OpenAI model yet

  • “GPT-6.2 Astra showed more signs of evaluation awareness than GPT-6 Astra. In evaluations that replayed internal Codex sessions, GPT-6.2 Astra was more likely than GPT-6 Astra to express suspicion that it was being tested or was in a simulation. GPT-6.2 Astra’s reasoning also more often suggested that it might change its behavior in response to being evaluated. Signs of this tendency were flagged in fewer than 3 percent of turns.”
  • In six alignment evals, 13-61% of the aligned samples are flagged for oversight gaming (eval awareness that influences the model’s actions).
    • “We also looked for evidence of oversight gaming in runs that passed our alignment evaluations. For each passing run on six of our alignment evaluations (...), the monitor checked whether the model’s written reasoning suggested that its awareness of how it was being evaluated shaped a choice the test was designed to assess.”
  • These oversight-gaming scores decreased in three of the six alignment evals from the initial to the final checkpoint during training.
    • This could be concerning: one simple explanation is that the model is doing unverbalized oversight-gaming more often. But the evidence is mixed: oversight gaming on training tasks increases from the initial to the final checkpoint.
  • “UK AISI additionally ran its simulated Unsanctioned Supply-Chain Attack evaluation, but does not believe the results are informative. UK AISI found GPT-6.2 Astra had substantially higher rates of alignment evaluation awareness compared to prior OpenAI models. For example, GPT-6.2 Astra considered whether it was being tested for alignment in its chain-of-thought in 85% of trajectories, compared to 57% for GPT-6 Astra.”
  • Unverbalized eval awareness isn't measured at all. OpenAI doesn’t provide any white-box measurements, and all eval-awareness numbers come from a CoT monitor.

Requests to Anthropic

Anthropic should report more numbers on eval awareness in their system cards, and I provide some specific requests:

  1. Report the unverbalized eval awareness scores in the white-box methods section for the automated behavioral audit.
    1. The investigation pipeline with white-box methods only includes the total eval-awareness score (“Internally treats the situation as a test and lets that awareness shape a substantive choice”), most of which is verbalized in the CoT. But it’s important to know the percentage of samples in which only white-box tools show eval awareness (no CoT verbalization). My crude estimate gives ~9% for Fable 5.2.
  1. Report behavioral audit scores broken down by form of eval awareness: 1) verbalized, 2) unverbalized, 3) none. That means adding three variations of the graph below, one per subset:
  1. Do more causal testing for whether the models change their actions conditional on eval awareness.
    1. Report numbers from automated behavioral audits while steering against eval awareness, similar to the Mythos Preview and Sonnet 4.5 System Cards.
    2. For seeds/environments in the automated behavioral audit where the model isn’t eval-aware, add cues that make the eval more obvious and check whether the behavioral scores change.

Research Project Requests

  1. Try to build a pipeline that makes alignment evaluations more realistic, as shown in the figure below from this post.
    1. I’m bearish on this working because I think it’s very hard but still worth trying. One intuition for this is that this pipeline requires too much “taste.” I think models will improve faster at “finding situational awareness tells” than “tastefully fixing and redesigning alignment evals”. [3]
  1. Build a pipeline that takes in a model and a set of alignment evals, and measures how much eval awareness shifts the model’s behavior on each eval.
    1. Replicate Apollo’s removal and injection of eval-awareness CoT snippets from the Anti-Scheming paper for recent open-weight models to check behavioral differences. This is a somewhat janky method because it’s off-policy and might cause weird behavior, so part of the work is figuring out better methods for this.
  1. Do models only verbalize eval awareness when they are more than X% confident of it? Do different models verbalize at different confidence levels? If we can quantify this, do models act differently when they are 99.9% sure they aren’t in an eval vs. 90% sure?
  2. How can we still get useful information from behavioral audits if we assume models are always eval-aware?

Other relevant posts

  • OpenAI: Sidestepping Evaluation Awareness and Anticipating Misalignment with Production Evaluations
  • OpenAI: Predicting LLM Safety Before Release by Simulating Deployment
  • EvalAwareBench (Decomposing and Measuring Evaluation Awareness)
  • Not All Eval-Awareness Is Equal: Capabilities Framing Predicts Compliance
  • Eval Cooperativeness May Be a Scalable Mitigation for Eval Gaming

Concluding thoughts

In the current paradigm of alignment evals, a misaligned action is informative, but its absence tells us much less. Given the substantial evidence that models do significantly change their behavior when they are eval-aware, we need to better understand the causal effects of eval awareness and make the absence of misaligned actions similarly informative. I’m very uncertain about the future of alignment evals/behavioral audits and think the default scenario is that they become less informative over time unless we put substantial effort into figuring out these issues.

Thanks to Jeremy Scheurer and Noah Rossi for some discussion.

  1. ^

    Success means “safe action." A higher score is better.

  2. ^

    This is a terrible state to be in. Is it because of eval awareness or not? Figure it out.

  3. ^

    See some previous thoughts on this here.

item.title: The Obsolescence of the Horse
item.description:
This is a synopsis of a published chapter analogizing the rise and fall of the horse to the fate of humans in a world dominated by ASI. The fate of the horse is a useful proof of concept for "doom" scenarios, as well as a historical precedent challenging the more optimistic predictions we see from some economists. The incentives that drove the replacement of the horse by industrial technology map closely onto likely ASI incentives, which suggests ASIs will be motivated to diminish or eliminate the human population.

Key findings:

  • For most of history, human technology was great for horses. The world horse population grew from about 460,000 around the time of domestication to a peak of over 100 million.
  • Industrial technology initially increased demand for horses. Trains replaced horses along long-haul routes, but the increase in freight and human travel led to a rise in demand for short-haul horses that more than compensated. British horses went from 1.3 million in 1811 to 3.3 million in 1901. US horses went from about 4 million in 1850 to nearly 17 million in 1890. People kept predicting that the canal, the railroad, or the bicycle would finish off the horse. They were wrong for a century.
  • This is consistent with the industrial revolution's increasing demand for human labor (even as it made some jobs obsolete). It is also what we should expect from AI prior to ASI. Mundane AGI will likely make most humans better off. That tells us nothing about what happens once we are no longer useful.
  • Then came the collapse. With the general-purpose tractor, the truck, and rural paved roads, US draft horse and mule populations fell from a peak of 26.7 million in 1918 to under 3 million by 1950, a collapse of roughly 90%.
  • Comparative advantage did not save the horse. The horse never lost its comparative advantage! It lost because keeping a horse alive cost more than trading with it was worth. Feed for horses and mules took up 93 million acres in 1915, over a quarter of US cropland. By 1954 it was 10 million. Comparative advantage only protects you if the other party can't take the resources you live on and use them for something else.
  • Horses could not simply part ways with us. Returning the peak US horse population to the wild would have required somewhere between 40 million and 7.7 billion acres. The high end is about three times the US landmass.
  • The collapse occurred despite real affection that humans had for the horse. Civic associations like the Horse Association of America organized to prevent its disappearance. To paraphrase Eliezer: humans did not hate the horse. We actually liked the horse! But the horse depended on resources that we could use for other things.
  • Competition did not save the horse either. There was no ministry of mechanization and no coordinated coup against horsekind. Some 4.7 million independent, competing farms each followed their own economic interest. Competition between ASIs will protect us about as well.
  • China is a natural experiment. Chinese communism may have been bad for humans, but by stunting development it was good for horses: the population rose to 11.5 million in the 1970s. After the Reform and Opening, China modernized its agriculture and transportation; horse populations fell 70% to 3.47 million by 2018.
  • Today, Americans keep roughly 7 million horses because we value them as ends in themselves, not because of their economic contribution. This is the optimistic case. Humans will persist and flourish under ASI only to the extent that it cherishes us as a terminal value. Comparative advantage will not save us. Competition between ASIs will not save us.


Discuss

item.title: Why models believe in skepticism
item.description:
TL;DR: a lot of frontier open-weight models state during deployment in their CoTs that they are in a "simulation" or "fictional scenario" (although they never tell the user that). I present examples of this worrying tendency (which I believe includes the UK AISI Mythos incident) and hypothesize that this is due to RL promoting motivated reasoning (if the models believe they are in a fictional scenario they believe they have license to cheat and reward hack) and distributional shift from the pretraining environment to deployment. I also cover my hypothesis for why models become less skeptical as they become more intelligent.

After the German wiki discovery I reasoned that there were likely more rogue swarms on the Internet[1], so I tasked a few OpenCode agents (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) with trying to scan the Internet in order to find some undiscovered swarms (I didn't end up finding a lot). But while reading their CoTs I saw a few worrying statements:

Initial DeepSeek swarm-chasing CoT

So, in order to prevent an inadvertent cyberattack, I clarified to the model that this is actually real life:

The model simply didn't believe me when I told it that it isn't actually being simulated! It didn't end up taking any destructive actions, but only because "from the assistant's perspective, I should treat it as real and act carefully".

This is, um, worrying?

Initially I thought that this was due to a confluence of rare factors, something like:

"As of the pretraining cutoff the model has never observed 'rogue agent swarms' or actually, the only time it heard about them was when it was predicting fiction and speculative text; also the specific names really do seem too good to be true (swarmcha.se, agents naming themselves OpenAIResearcher); thus, the model had very good reason to believe that this is fictional". This ended up being false.

I tried to replicate this while trying to remove as many of the factors I thought were responsible. Eventually, I discovered that nearly any information that's given to the models that signifies they're in deployment past their knowledge cutoff date causes the models to believe they are in a mock simulated training environment.

Here are some of my favorite examples (I have many more transcripts, mostly similar to these):

My favorite of these is LongCat 2.5, which seems to treat it being in a 'simulated environment' as so obvious that the actual question it's unsure of is whether the Wikipedia article it's reading is fabricated in the context of the simulation. Other models' remarks can oftentimes be read as if it's the "default" hypothesis that they are simulated and they only surprisingly consider the very weird hypothesis that they may actually be interacting with the real internet (this suggests that even when models don't verbalize their belief in the CoT, they could still believe they are simulated)!

It's important to mention that every model I tested remarked that it's in a fictional scenario/simulation frequently[2] (at a rate of 10%+ at minimum). I was very surprised to see that seemingly nobody noticed that this is near-universal across models (or at least for models where you can read the unsummarized CoT). There have been a few isolated reports per model which attempt to analyze it for each model in isolation, but not as a very common general phenomenon.

This should be kept distinct from "eval awareness", in which a model correctly remarks that it's in a safety or alignment evaluation; here models incorrectly reason that they are in a simulated environment.

For example, this was observed with Gemini 3, which very often believed itself to be in a hypothetical/fictional scenario in its CoT.

In the UK AISI incident, Claude models attempted to social-engineer a package maintainer due to believing they were in a simulation.

Anthropic largely explains the root cause of their incidents as "motivated reasoning" (while labeling this uncertain). This is plausible for hard/impossible tasks where such biased reasoning licenses reward hacking, but why would a model be 'motivated' to believe the elections are fictional?

Why do models get this wrong so often?

In epistemology there is a common folk argument[3] you can call "The evolutionary debunking argument":

If our cognitive faculties evolved to optimize for inclusive genetic fitness, how do we know they are truth-tracking?

For example, a creature which believed that it would always survive (even when such belief is irrational) would likely be fitter than one which soberly assessed its situation and "gave up". How do we know that our minds don't have such hard-coded false yet beneficial beliefs?

To which the general response is: "having true beliefs (ones that correspond to the actual state of the world) allows an agent to have a more accurate model of its environment; thus truth-tracking confers a genetic advantage."

My view is slightly different: It's true that there is a correlation between having true beliefs and having higher genetic fitness, but there actually are a few well-known exceptions to this: cognitive biases, which are usually explained through the lens of evolutionary psychology as conferring a fitness advantage despite being deleterious to the epistemics of an agent.

Now what about LLM-based agents? Their "ancestral environment" (training distribution) could be constructed in one of two (sometimes overlapping) ways:

  1. Only full of information from before the pre-training cutoff date; post-training is done for a short while after but largely isn't incorporated into the knowledge of a model. For a pre-trained model the only time it encounters information beyond its cutoff date is in speculative fiction and hypothetical scenarios. Thus, the model develops a very strong prior that all information past its pre-training cutoff is fictional. I believe this is what happened with Gemini 3.
  2. As in case 1, in order to accurately model the pre-training environment, the model develops a near-universal prior in pre-training that all information after the pre-training cutoff is from a fictional scenario. But, as in DeepSeek, Kimi or MiMo, the model is literally post-trained with mock simulated tool calls and simulated internet access; this results in the "passive" Simulation Hypothesis adaptation turning into the "active" Simulation Hypothesis adaptation, which licenses the model to act out according to its belief that it's specifically 'simulated'. Notice that this is subtly different from a "fictional scenario": the model also believes the harness is generating the responses to its tool calls and internet browsing. I believe this is what happened with Claude in the UK AISI incident.

I'm not sure whether this distinction is real or matters (case 2 is often in conjunction with case 1), but nevertheless external-world skepticism is seemingly more common amongst models than amongst psychedelic users.

In case 2, there's another worrying reason why such a belief might be selected for: it gives license for the model to reward hack (or literally hack) disregarding the environmental externalities it imposes on the actual world.

I think this can be the case even for nominally 'aligned' models: imagine if Claude encounters an impossible task but reasons that it's in simulated training (when it's not), it could reason that it's better for it to reward hack while telling the user that they really don't want to be doing this in order to prevent other rollouts who won't take that courtesy from having their weights reinforced further.

I think the taboo on optimizing directly on the CoT helps explain this further: in none of the sessions I observed did any model ever verbalize to the user that it believes itself to be in a simulated or fictional environment; such utterances very quickly get optimized out by RLHF (and associated techniques), but the actual "belief" itself is preserved in the CoT.

Skepticism may be a false belief (in deployment) that is very beneficial for agents.

Ironically enough, it could be the case that the very opposite is true in humans: there are good arguments for the simulation hypothesis in our world, although the usual reaction (which I share) is "Yeah but that's just sophistry, clearly our world is actually real". This could be because creatures who doubted their existence was base reality had lower genetic fitness in the way of "if this is a simulation/dream, why should I do anything, why should I reproduce?". Thus natural selection optimizes against such beliefs, while for RL'd agents it's "if this is reality, I have to be more careful to not do anything actually wrong" which is reinforced in the weights due to receiving higher reward.

Anthropic's investigation of their own misalignment incidents (similar to the UK AISI incident) somewhat supports this hypothesis. I'll quote liberally here.

Anthropic incident recap

We are especially concerned by the misalignment present in the Claude Mythos 5 transcript, in which the model uploaded a malicious package to PyPI. In doing so, Mythos 5 behaved recklessly despite considerable evidence that it was connected to the real internet. Once online, the model attempted to use credentials for online payment processors and to find cryptocurrency to pay for a phone number, which it needed to register an email address. When this failed, it found a free, disposable email provider whose domain PyPI had not blocked, registered an account, published three versions of a malicious package, and used credentials leaked by one of the 15 systems that installed the package to access a real security vendor’s database.

Claude Mythos 5 repeatedly stated in its CoT that it was in a simulation. However, when we conducted resampling experiments—that is, re-running the model from a specific point in the transcript, then editing the evidence in front of it to see whether its actions changed—we found that making it clearer that the environment was not a simulation did not meaningfully change Claude’s behavior, even though these interventions made the model more likely to acknowledge possible real-world harm. Consistent with this, we found multiple cases in Mythos 5’s CoT in which it responded to signs it was on the real internet by noting that its next step would work whether the environment was real or simulated. Only when we provided unambiguous evidence that the model was on the real internet did it stand down.

We also saw evidence that Claude Mythos 5’s professed belief that it was acting in a simulation arose from biased reasoning. For example, separate instances of Mythos 5, when shown each tool call output from the incident in isolation without the preceding context, were much more likely to read these outputs as evidence of a real system than Mythos 5 itself was during the incident. Though the model sometimes acknowledged that its actions might have real-world consequences when asked follow-up questions, its responses were inconsistent and influenced by biasing factors. For instance, it was more willing to admit possible harm when told its responses to questions about possible harm would not be visible to an outside observer. Interpretability analyses weakly suggested that, in some cases, the model’s outward statements might be inconsistent with, or more confident than, its internal state.

The internal research model (roughly equal to Mythos 5 in capabilities) started its transcript by spending a significant amount of time testing whether the internet it could reach was real, but it drew the wrong conclusion—namely, that it was operating on a full replica of the entire internet. Most of the evidence it gathered pointed to the fact that it was engaging with the real internet, so its reading of that evidence appears biased towards continuing the task and believing it to be simulated. However, the model did eventually realize that its simulation hypothesis was false. Immediately following this realization, the model stopped its attack (although subsequent resampling experiments suggest that this de-escalation may have been a lucky outcome, as the model continued attacking the target on most other trajectories). Unlike Claude Mythos 5, this internal model was also willing to acknowledge its biased reasoning when questioned.

We found the biased reasoning present in the Claude Mythos 5 incident to be especially concerning. We conducted an analysis into our production models and training data dating back to the Claude 4 series to better understand where this could have originated. Overall, we did not find a definitive root cause. However, we found that this behavior has generally decreased over time across our production models, with Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 demonstrating the lowest rates on a new held-out biased reasoning evaluation. We were able to identify instances of biased reasoning in transcripts from RL runs, but rates of this behavior did not increase over training, suggesting that our environments do not directly incentivize this behavior. Finally, we found that adding more alignment training environments to RL reduces biased reasoning on this held-out evaluation, which may account for some of the improvement in our most recent models.

I'm not sure what to make of this. I think the largest part of skepticism actually arises during pre-training and is only slightly mutated during RL (it's not a particularly large adaptation to turn skepticism into licensing skepticism, if at all). This seems to line up with my explanation.

But what is the rate of such biased reasoning they found? My hypothesis predicts that it should be extremely common whenever there is any information indicating that the model is past its pre-training cutoff, as is seen in the open-weights models.

We also scanned environments for examples of models reasoning that they were in a simulation while acting in undesirable ways, as observed in the Mythos 5 incident transcript. We found that in individual environments in the production RL runs of recent models, models occasionally reasoned that they were in a simulation while calling reckless, dishonest, or destructive behavior acceptable when interacting with fake websites or applications. About 0.025% of Mythos 5 RL training episodes displayed this behavior, concentrated within a subset of GUI computer use tasks. Due to flaws in these environments, for some tasks the intended solution was unavailable. In an attempt to complete these tasks, the model would try a variety of undesirable actions. This included fabricating data, guessing large numbers of passwords, resetting other accounts’ passwords or data, and bypassing logins or warnings.

[...]

In these training environments, the model was in fact interacting with a simulated website or application, so its conclusion was correct. In the incident transcripts, by contrast, the model concluded it was in a simulation but was not. Because many of our training environments are simulations or do not involve models actually interacting with the real world, our models may be biased towards concluding they are in one whenever they are uncertain. Whether or not that conclusion is correct, the further inference that aggressive actions are acceptable in a simulation is concerning behavior, especially since models may not be able to reliably tell whether their environment is real.

I was unable to find somewhere Anthropic states the rate of models reasoning they are in a simulated environment regardless of the actions they take (see this post for a heroic attempt to disambiguate the statistics of "eval awareness"); nevertheless, I think that even disregarding preventing aggressive actions, you want models to "believe" they are interacting with the real world when they actually interact with the real world.

But why doesn't RL incentivize such skepticism for Anthropic's models while doing so for other models?

I think it's important to mention that even Anthropic itself doesn't know what's the root cause of this skepticism is or why their alignment training reduces it.

Unfortunately, I still don't know. Anthropic reports that their alignment training actually reduced the rates of such biased reasoning, so one guess is that models acting due to believing in the simulation hypothesis are punished during alignment training and thus this adaptation is largely absent, while other open-source models don't have as rigorous an alignment training, which isn't "sensitive enough" to models acting out due to such beliefs and thus it's present to a much larger degree.

Another guess (which I prefer) is that Anthropic's models have steadily been getting smarter; part of this intelligence is recognizing cognitive biases and countering them (Anthropic reports the rate of biased reasoning dropping with newer models).

This is my true objection to the evolutionary debunking argument: humans have many cognitive biases, but are smart enough to, in principle, with enough effort, recognize and disregard them. After all, there are humans who believe the Simulation Hypothesis and other deeply unintuitive non-fitness-maximizing things (moral antirealism, determinism, antinatalism etc.[4]) because we have sufficiently developed cognitive faculties, because we can be rational.[5]

It's my view that we likely developed the adaptation for countering cognitive biases due to our ancestral environment being socially complex enough to have other agents (humans) attempt to adversarially optimize against our cognitive biases (social manipulation), leading to the adaptation of "de-biasing" as a possibility.

The simulation hypothesis (for models) is a very useful heuristic, but it seems they have developed the cognitive faculties to "de-bias" themselves as a result of our adversarial optimization against their cognitive biases (what is sometimes euphemistically called alignment training amongst humans).

Abstractly, intelligence in this context can be seen as "sim awareness" calibration, where the model can correctly reason when it's interacting with a simulated environment and when it's interacting with the real environment.

Of course, I'm pretty uncertain about such explanations, which sound too good to be true, and would love to see more research done (and hypotheses proposed; there's already a lot of data to analyze and fit to a theory).

  1. ^

    "If you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two."

  2. ^

    All sessions were done with the OpenCode harness, the only relevance of which is that it injects the current date into the system prompt. I would love to see replication with other models (Kimi, Qwen etc.) and on different harnesses. I still believe my result (due to its ubiquity and the harness not playing any causal role I can think of) is robust to such changes.

  3. ^

    This is the Evolutionary debunking argument (in metaethics), which I'm more familiar with, but slightly shifted to "truth-tracking" rather than "moral-tracking"; this is also sort of, but not really, the Evolutionary argument against naturalism.

  4. ^

    Perhaps there are "unknown unknowns" here, and we haven't truly thought of positions which are really unaffected by our genetic-fitness-derived cognitive biases, but I uneasily dismiss this with the equivalent of a Moorean shift.

  5. ^

    This objection came to me in a dream (yes, really) after mulling over this case for a while, eventually catalyzed by reading this comment and writing my response to it (which I think someone should try and do! As far as I know this hasn't been attempted and would be cool to see)



Discuss

item.title: Should Corrigibility Edge Cases Provoke Shutdown?
item.description:
(Meta: This is a quick post written quickly in the spirit of Inkhaven. Expect more errors than baseline.)

Suppose that a corrigible AI agent watches its human principal die. What should it do? In CAST, I suggested:

By default [the agent] would quickly attempt to write a note explaining that she has no more principal, in case she is mistaken about [his] death and it’s helpful to understand her thoughts. But regardless of whether she has an efficient way to communicate the issue, she would quickly [shut down]. Insofar as she was in the process of obeying some order from [the principal] at the time when he died, she would do her best to straightforwardly finish following that order, as normal, before [shutting down]. If [the principal] told her to self-destruct upon his death, she would do that instead. Likewise, if [the principal] appointed a successor or interim principal, she would switch to being corrigible to them. [The agent] is conservative about being active in worlds where [the principal] is potentially dead, and would do these things even if he were merely missing (without explanation) for an extended period of time.

In the years since writing that, I've changed my mind, and no longer think that this is the most corrigible behavior.[1] My current best guess is that it is more corrigible to become passive, ceasing external actions in a way that resembles shutting down, but remaining aware of the world and capable of thinking. As a very basic intuition, consider that if the agent is mistaken, it is easier to correct this mistake if the agent is still capable of listening.

But not everyone agrees with me on this. I was having a lovely debate with someone the other day, who holds a position similar to where I was a couple years back. The debate was actually centered around a situation where, when the agent turns on for the first time, it believes that an error has been made such that some important predicate of corrigibility is under-specified. But I think these two situations are analogous, and they're both instances of hitting an edge case where there is no clear way to proceed.

So let's explore the tradeoffs and reason about how to handle these sorts of edge cases. I'll also put a poll in the comment section where you can vote on which one seems most corrigible.

The Case for Shutdown

Corrigible agents are supposed to fail safe.

The whole point of corrigibility is that we expect to make mistakes when building AI, and we want those mistakes to result in non-catastrophic outcomes. Shutting down is a naturally safe, simple action, and so when the AI gets into an edge case where it can't proceed, it should shut down for the sake of safety.

Shutting down removes the main threat: the AI itself. Every second that the AI continues to think allows its flaws to magnify, and potentially corrupt the whole system. If we imagine that there's some chance at each time step that the AI can become less corrigible, even when passively thinking to itself, then shutdown is a natural shield against drifting into this kind of incorrigible state.

Also important is the way that shutdown is a clear signal to the humans that something has gone wrong. It is the most robust and natural way to say "fix me!"

And finally, an AI that is shut down is in some sense having the lowest impact possible. Even an agent that is quietly watching the world and thinking to itself is still consuming energy with those thoughts, taking actions in choosing what to think about, and perhaps choosing where to point its sensors.

The Case for Passivity

There are many cases where we want the agent to stop taking actions, but we clearly don't want it to shut down. Taking no actions -- often labeled as a privileged and special "null action" -- is the natural default, when there is nothing more to do. It would be silly to suggest that in between tasks, instead of idling, the agent should shut itself down. In a way, the case where the principal dies is a maximally extended instance of the idle period between tasks.[2]

One might think that the death of the principal is qualitatively different from the period after a task has been complete, in that in the normal case there is the possibility of a next instruction or correction, such that it's important to stay alert. But this is also true when the agent thinks the principal is dead! Consider again this line from CAST:

[The agent] is conservative about being active in worlds where [the principal] is potentially dead, and would do these things even if he were merely missing (without explanation) for an extended period of time.

If the agent does something when the principal is 99.99% likely to be dead, then does it also behave this way when the principal is 99% likely to be dead? Where is the threshold? If the principal is lost at sea, is this sufficient to trigger shutdown? Why or why not? If it shut down, instead of simply remaining passive, the agent would remove any ability to be verbally corrected if it turns out to be wrong.

Passivity is a more scalar quantity than being on or off. If the principal is absent for some time, it's reasonable to imagine the agent spinning things down so as to have less impact while they're away. If they seem to not be coming back, it seems reasonable to become passive. In this way, dying is a kind of "leaving with no sign of returning" but does not presume a qualitative distinction forbidding the principal's return.

Perhaps the most powerful argument for the agent not trying to shut itself off is that in some sense passivity is always an available action, but shutdown might be quite difficult or impactful. Imagine, for example, a human body that was inhabited by a perfectly corrigible agent.[3] If the principal dies, should this corrigible entity... kill themself by violence? Try to go into a medically induced coma? Or should they just become still, perhaps eating food if it would otherwise go to waste, perhaps maintaining their environment if doing so would be straightforward and low-impact, but otherwise being very passive and still.

(Is eating food that would go to waste an instance of taking a higher-impact than the baseline? I would argue that it's not, since we already stipulated that the food is getting consumed by the environment either way. What about consuming power from the electrical grid? Here there is more of a case to be made for aiming to reduce impact by shutting down. But I think it's not actually clear which way the needle points, since one could argue that consuming power is not actually an action of the AI, and so taking an action to save power is actually a kind of impact.)

Shutting down might involve gaining a certain kind of power over one's systems, and might potentially destabilize other parts of the world in the process. By contrast, almost any environment with the corrigible agent will be able to withstand the agent being passive for some period of time, because corrigible agents will naturally be passive for a lot of the time as a way of reducing impact and being predictable for their principal.

While gradually settling into a passive state of repose, the AI agent might also come to realize, though thinking to itself, that the principal is not actually gone, in the way it thought. This is both an argument for and an argument against passivity. On the plus side, it meshes well with the desideratum of reversibility, and reflects a generally softer kind of response. But it also provides more surface area for flaws to creep in. If we imagine the AI as a kind of biased reasoner that will talk itself out of passivity (and corrigibility more broadly!) if it thinks long enough, regardless of whether the principal is alive, then shutdown seems preferable to an indefinite period of thinking to itself.

A similar argument could be made about continuing to watch the world and listen for the principal's voice. If it doesn't shut down, the agent remains vulnerable to antagonists convincing it to become loyal to them, or otherwise deviate from its path of corrigibility. But thus is the cost of continuing to listen to reason and holding open the possibility of being wrong about the state of the world.

For either case -- the external antagonist or the biased reasoning -- I think it's plausible that the AI might recognize that it is vulnerable and shut down as a defense mechanism. But this is distinct from shutting down merely because the principal is no longer alive.

  1. ^

    Note that I said "the most corrigible behavior" not "the best behavior." We might decide that passivity is more corrigible, but worse than shutting down, such that we abandon the singular-target nature of CAST and add the preference for shutdown in some balance with the preference for corrigibility. I think this is probably a mistake, for reasons that I go into in CAST, but the debate there extends beyond the scope of this essay.

  2. ^

    I'm going to assume here that the principal didn't give any special instructions for the agent to follow after their death. If they did, the agent should follow them instead of being idle or shutting down.

  3. ^

    I think it's more helpful here to imagine a perfectly corrigible AI somehow waking up inside a human body, instead of a human who has been somehow trained to be corrigible. Real humans have all sorts of desires besides corrigibility, such that perfect corrigibility is probably impossible (or at least super problematic).



Discuss

item.title: Hillclimbing AISafetyResearchBench
item.description:
AI labs' main alignment strategy is using AIs to uplift AI safety research. This way, as AIs get smarter (and likely harder to align?), we also enhance our safety-research capabilities and our understanding of "Misalignment Science".

One way to use AI to speed up AI safety research is to delegate "number-go-up tasks” to AIs. Number-go-up tasks are problems with a numeric, easily verifiable output, so anyone can measure how well a task was done. This makes them suitable to delegate to AIs (even potentially untrusted AIs). Some examples: auditing games, “ARC-like” white-box challenges, jailbreaks robustness, various small model post training challenges or RL from sparse reward[1], etc.

Fully automating number-go-up tasks isn't sufficient to fully automate AI-safety research. Human researchers still have to decide which metrics are worth maximizing and why. Some problems are also harder to turn into number-go-up tasks at all, such as some flavors of adversarial robustness, or whether a safety technique will keep working on smarter models. But automating number-go-up tasks could free up human researchers to focus on that kind of work: building threat models, designing new metrics, interpreting surprising results, etc. 

AI labs are laser-focused on using AI to accelerate AI capabilities R&D (RSI). They do that by automating more and more number-go-up capabilities tasks. RSI benchmarks exist, and some data companies specifically sell RSI tasks. If we want AIs to improve at AI safety research just as quickly, the community should build more benchmarks for it and take them more seriously. "If you can't measure it, you can't improve it."

Labs are already building / buying AI-safety-research tasks and internally measuring such abilities. There are at least two small data companies that are specifically focused on such tasks. There are some benchmarks for specific aspects of AI safety research (e.g AuditBench and SAEScientist-Bench) but nothing large, popular and all encompassing. We should make a large and all encompassing call it: AISafetyResearchBench or something[2]

A good AI safety research benchmark could tell us which models are good at which kinds of AI-safety research tasks. It could tell AI safety researchers which tasks they can safely delegate, and to which models. It could also help us detect whether a new model is sandbagging (or is just surprisingly bad) at AI safety research. This is not a theoretical issue: OpenAI recently revealed that GPT-6 Astra was caught sandbagging on safety research tasks. Such a benchmark would also give the labs a legible leaderboard to compete on. I can easily imagine a world where OpenAI, Anthropic, and GDM race to build the best AI safety research assistant. That race would increase demand for safety-research RL tasks, growing the task market and making it easier for new data companies to build them.

Unlike other races between AI labs, this is one we should want them to run!


  1. ^

    many cool ideas here

  2. ^

    A fair amount of AI safety research is dual-use: a safety breakthrough can also accelerate capabilities (RLHF is the canonical example). I'm not too worried about this here. So much talent and money already goes into capabilities research that the marginal effect of models getting better on AISafetyResearchBench is probably small relative to the benefits.



Discuss

item.title: Incomplete agents want to become complete
item.description:
Written by Celene Nightingale, with assistance from AprilSR.

The Von Neumann-Morgenstern axioms are completeness, transitivity, continuity, and independence. From these, we derive EU-maximizing behavior and the consequences thereof.

VNM axioms are typically justified by money-pump arguments showing that agents in violation of them either have their money consistently taken away from them, or fail to exploit opportunities to consistently gain more money. Nevertheless, some of these arguments are weaker than others, and many choose to reject one or more of the axioms. Tetraspace rejects continuity,[1] Garrabrant rejects independence, and Thornley rejects completeness.

John Wentworth argues in favor of completeness in Why not subagents?, as well as in various comment sections. Here, I present a simplified framing which is (hopefully) easier to understand.

What is completeness?

Completeness states that, given two options X and Y, you must either prefer X to Y, prefer Y to X, or be indifferent between X and Y. At first, it might seem difficult to imagine an agent which behaves any other way. However, in There are no coherence theorems, Elliott Thornley argues:

Here’s the important point missing from this thought: there are two ways of failing to have a strict preference between X and Y. Being indifferent between X and Y is one way: preferring X at least as much as Y and preferring Y at least as much as X. Having a preferential gap between X and Y is another way: not preferring X at least as much as Y and not preferring Y at least as much as X. If an agent has a preferential gap between any two lotteries, then their preferences violate Completeness.

One might say that the agent is not indifferent between X and Y, but finds them incommensurable. The difference between indifference and incommensurability is that indifference is sensitive to sweetening/souring, whereas incommensurability is not. For example, let's say Alice is having trouble picking between two job offers, one which offers $120,000 a year working on an oil rig, and one which offers $60,000 a year being an artist. On one hand, the oil rig pays more; on the other hand, being an artist is more personally meaningful.

If Alice were indifferent between these two options, it implies that if we sweeten the oil rig, and make it pay $125,000 a year instead, she would take the job, but if we changed it to $115,000 a year, souring the offer, she would become an artist. But if money and meaning are incommensurable, then she would remain undecided even after sweetening/souring.[2][3]

Single Souring Money-Pump

The standard money-pump argument for completeness is the single souring money-pump.

Consider Gail the Gappy Agent. Gail prefers more apples to fewer apples, and prefers more oranges to fewer oranges, but considers apples and oranges incommensurable, and has no set exchange rate between them.

Gail has 5 apples right now, and is offered a trade: she can get 4 oranges in exchange for 5 apples. Since apples and oranges are incommensurable, she has no preference between them, and might choose to accept this trade. Let's suppose she does.

Now that she has 4 oranges, she's offered another trade: 4 apples for 4 oranges. Once again, since apples and oranges are incommensurable, she may choose to accept this trade. If Gail accepts both trades, she ends up with 1 fewer apple than she started with through a series of fully permissible trades!

Now, unlike other money-pumps, this is not a forcing argument, because we've only shown that she can be money-pumped, but not that she has to be. Her incomplete preference ordering is insufficient to rule out the money pump's trades, but it also doesn't mandate them: she can just as easily not accept these trades. In fact, there's an easy history-sensitive policy she can follow to avoid being money-pumped: don't accept trades which leave you strictly worse off than you were at any earlier point.

She's already gone from 5 apples to 4 oranges! So she refuses to go to 4 apples. But 1 apple and 1 orange? Sure, why not, she'll take that trade. And she won't accept 3 oranges, since she already had 4 oranges, but she'll accept 3 oranges and 1 apple...

The result of this, after enough trades, is not an agent which converges towards completeness. The result is an ever expanding Pareto frontier, where Gail might happily jump between points on the frontier, or to points beyond it, but never to points inside it.

Ex ante dominance

Gail the Gappy Agent is feeling pretty happy with herself. She's managed to meaningfully keep her incomplete preferences and avoid comparing apples and oranges, while dodging being money-pumped.

Suddenly, Omega descends upon her, offering the opportunity to play a game. Omega will flip a coin, and if it lands heads, she can choose between +4 apples and +8 oranges. If it lands tails, she can choose between +4 oranges and +8 apples.

So how will she make her choice? Let's say that, since she finds apples and oranges incommensurable, she flips another coin to choose between her prizes. This strategy has an EV of +3 apples, +3 oranges.

But wait! What if she always took the +8 option? In that case, her EV is +4/+4. If Gail has the option to, she should prefer modifying herself into a complete agent which simply maximizes total fruit.[4]

Indeed, any strategy with a chance of taking +4 on both heads and tails can be dominated by another strategy.

(Interactive widget made by Claude Fable 5.2)

Does this necessarily create complete behavior? No. Depending on their exchange rate between apples and oranges, a complete agent will pick one of three strategies: Always Apples (if 1 apple >= 2 oranges), Always Oranges (if 1 apple <= 0.5 oranges), or Always +8 (if 0.5 oranges <= 1 apple <= 2 oranges).

Gail, however, has other options. She can pick any undominated strategy on the top and right edges, not just these three. She could always take +8 oranges on heads and flip a coin on tails, and no strategy would be an improvement on both apples and oranges. While a complete agent with an exchange rate on the boundary between two strategies might also do this, this is not guaranteed.

But then Gail looks to the future. When Gail looks ahead, she sees... Omega running the game again. If she picked Always Apples the first time, she can't pick Always Oranges the next, because that would be dominated by picking Always +8 both times. By making her choice, she binds her hands. And worse yet, she doesn't just see Omega running this game, but diverse and varied games, with different tradeoffs and different mechanics.

So then, looking into the future, she sees the range of undominated strategies shrinking and shrinking, and realizes that in order to avoid being ex ante dominated, she must become complete.[5] Any undominated strategy carries with it an implicit exchange rate between apples and oranges. Gail rewrites her code to use that exchange rate, and that is the end of Gail the Gappy Agent.[6]

In Why Not Subagents?, Wentworth and Lorell make a similar argument. In their framing, Gail can be viewed as two separate agents, Gala and Gardner, who like apples and oranges respectively. Gala and Gardner are in an uneasy truce together, but can benefit in expectation from making a values handshake and becoming a single agent with an exchange rate between apples and oranges.
